utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Monday, the 4th of September, 2006. I'd like to say good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Good afternoon to Mr. Scott, as representative of the Prosecution. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel and to the accused. We would like to greet our witness who has been brought in the courtroom. Before we start hearing the witness, I'm first going to give the floor to Judge Trechsel, who will let you know about the Trial Chamber's position regarding an issue that was raised last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the name of the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Chamber found it necessary to make a comment to part of the hearing on Wednesday afternoon. It was page 79, on that day's transcript. I have not checked the present numbers, and it concerns a rather violent outburst of Mr. Karnavas at the address of Mr. Scott, where he used terms such as "sleazy" and, in particular, he said that the method of cross-examination used served to sneak information to the jury. Now, we're quite aware of such a possibility, that if the accusation asking the accused so you were at the street corner and you watched the accused coming in his red sports car around the corner at 4.45 in the afternoon, that is probably the type of thing Mr. Karnavas had in mind and with regard to such incidents, of course, the criticism is justified. However, I must stress I don't know for the how many'th time that this is not a trial with a jury. The Judges are aware of most of what is discussed here and that danger does not exist and there is no reason to get upset about it. And if one has a criticism, then the Chamber also believes that it should be uttered in appropriate terms, not by insinuating improper motives to the other party. This of course applies to both parties. I'm not saying that was the only incident so far, but my colleague Mr. Prandler has already commented at other opportunities on the style and atmosphere we like to maintain in this courtroom. The Chamber would very much like to have an atmosphere of a certain mutual respect even if one differs on the merits. I have been asked to make at that comment, and I have now done so. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This being said, I would like to add -- with regard to another incident that took place last week, I'd like to add the following: When Mr. Praljak spoke after the testimony of a witness, at that moment the credibility of the witness was questioned. The witness was even accused of having given a false testimony. On my personal behalf and on behalf of all the Judges, I'd like to remind Mr. Praljak that when he takes the floor he should do it properly and that in the future when Mr. Praljak wants to take the floor he will tell us first what he wants to talk about, what is the subject of his comments in order to avoid that type of situation. With regard of this particular incident I've mentioned, I'd like to remind Mr. Praljak and his counsel that it is always open to them to challenge the credibility of the witness or to question his testimony. You have two ways to go about it. The first way is to cross-examine the witness, and the second recourse you have is something that can happen later on when you bring your own witnesses. You can, through these witnesses, show that the Prosecution witness did not tell the truth, and you can prove that through your own witnesses. So before drawing conclusions about a specific witness, you need first to have produced further evidence. Last week the cross-examination took place but without any questions being asked about the truth of what the witness said. Later on you will have the possibility of bringing other witnesses who can tell us that on the specific day mentioned at paragraph 56 of the indictment, there were no troops of the HVO on site, and that even if 20 deaths have been recorded in the indictment, the facts did not happen as described in the indictment. But you have to prove that through your own witnesses. It's not enough to say that the witness lied. I wanted to add this to what my colleague had said. All the Judges have discussed the issue. So in the future, Mr. Praljak, you have to tell us, "I want to deal with such-and-such issue," and then we'll decide whether it's relevant or not. We have taken up five minutes in order for things to be very clear now. Today we are going to start hearing a new witness based on an expert report that has not been tendered yet. The Prosecution that is provided us with about -- with that pile of documents. That's about half a metre high. We even have more documents at the side there of the room, and we'll try to deal with this avalanche of documents. We'll now move on to the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you please rise. Before reading the solemn declaration, please give me your last name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomljanovich, William. 17th of May, 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation? What are your current functions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... officer in the investigations section of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, have you ever testified as an expert before this Tribunal? If that's the case, in what case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never before testified as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified in another capacity, as a regular witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I testified as a regular witness in the contempt proceedings against Markica Rebic in January, or was it February of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to ask you to read the solemn declaration that the usher is handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Very well. Witness, let me give you some information before we start your testimony. As you know, you're scheduled to testify for five days, five days of hearing. The Prosecution will have two days to put questions to you about a report -- about your report that has not been tendered yet but that everyone has read. Following the questions put to you during these two days by the Prosecution, the Defence will have three days to ask you questions as part of the cross-examination procedure. I do not yet know how they've organised themselves in terms of time sharing. Last week I invited them to think about it. If no agreement has been reached, the Chamber will have to rule about the way the time will be allocated to the various teams. As you perfectly know, you've drawn up a written report, and a number of exhibits will also be put to you during these two days. They will probably be tendered by the Prosecutor, these exhibits. I'd like to ask you to give very comprehensive and specific answers to the questions put to you by the Prosecutor and by the Defence counsel when time comes for the cross-examination, notwithstanding questions put by the Defence. So in due course, the four Judges who are sitting before you today can at any time intervene to answer questions to clarify some of your comments or some of your answers. It's a practice we have in this Chamber to ask questions because we want to be very clear, very specific about these matters. It's our responsibility at the end of the trial to render a judgement, and in the judgement we have to give our reasons. Therefore, we have to give very specific references to the witness statements, witness testimonies, and to all the exhibits produced during the testimony of the witness or following the testimony of a witness according to a procedure that we've put into place here. And since all of this might appear in the written judgement, we have to be extremely clear, extremely specific. So I would like to ask you to be very clear, very specific. This is what I wanted to tell you before we start, and without further ado I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, you will now proceed to the examination-in-chief. When you produce a document, in order to gain time, tell us, "Okay. This is document number 69, and I will later ask for this document to be tendered." Thus at the end we won't have to go through the list of exhibits everybody will be very clear about it right from the beginning. Mr. Murphy, you're on you're on your feet although we haven't started. I'm starting to worry myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President; good afternoon Your Honours. Now that the witness has been sworn in I want, if I may formally for the record, to interpose two objections to his testimony, and to make one oral application very briefly. The objections, firstly, are that the witness is not qualified to give expert testimony in the field of political science, which is essentially what he's being asked to do. And the second objection, Your Honours, one which Your Honours have already heard and ruled on, but just for the record, is that the witness being an employee of the Prosecutor and being closely involved with the preparation of the case should not be heard to be an expert witness even if he might testify on the facts. The oral application that I have, Your Honour, is this: Now that the Prosecution has committed Mr. Tomljanovich to testifying as an expert, it's quite clear as a matter of, I think, any domestic law and should be clear as a matter of the law of this Tribunal that any legal professional privilege or work product privilege in documents that he has generated or looked at in the course of preparing his opinion can no longer be sustained. It's one thing while he's still in the privacy of the office working as a member of the team, but once they commit him to testifying as an expert, the Defence should be entitled to see everything that underlies his opinion. So, Your Honour, my oral application is that the Prosecution, by tomorrow, disclose to the Defence all interoffice communications whether in the form of memoranda, e-mails, or otherwise that relate to any work that Mr. Tomljanovich has performed in connection either with his testimony, the formation of his opinion or his report, or indeed his work generally in preparing the case. That's my application, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Last week as you may recall I had made a suggestion or a request that at least with the preliminary matters a deposition be granted which could have been done on Friday, say, with the legal officer. That request was denied. In light of the time limitations, I have prepared a list of interrogatories which I wish to tender at this time. These are preliminary questions. I have a copy for every member of the Chamber as a well as for the registrar and the Prosecutor. I would like the gentleman to fill these out as if they're filled out under oath without the assistance of the Prosecution and to have them for us by -- by the time he's ready to be cross-examined. This would allow us, then, to have a more streamlined cross. I must apologise for not having them stapled, although they're -- I had to -- during the stapling process I made an error so I had to undo it, but it's in the correct order. And one other request. Following what Mr. Murphy had indicated, now that the gentleman is here on the stand, I would like an order that he is not to spend any time in his office or with the Prosecution while he's testifying. He should be treated like any other witness. So he should be forbidden to go into his office and have communications with his -- with his colleagues during the time that he's testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the interventions of Mr. Murphy and Mr. Karnavas, let me say the following: First of all, the Trial Chamber has decided that the witness would be heard as an expert witness. There's no way we are going to reconsider that ruling made by the Trial Chamber. Secondly, with respect to the application made by Mr. Murphy about the disclosure by the Prosecution of all interoffice memos, notes, instructions between the superiors of the expert at the Office of the Prosecutor and himself, we need to hear Mr. Scott about it. We need to hear Mr. Scott's response or comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution opposes both applications. We believe that the Defence of course has the right and opportunity to conduct extensive questioning on cross-examination within the bounds of both legality and propriety. The questions -- I haven't looked at Mr. Karnavas's interrogatories yet having just received them. There is no reason why to believe those questions if appropriate, if otherwise appropriate, cannot be put to the witness during cross-examination. I don't think there's any basis -- I don't know of any basis in the Rules to propound interrogatories to a witness in this fashion. So we oppose both applications. I think that counsel can make their own -- ask their own questions as to Mr. Tomljanovich's work at the OTP and his relation with me or with other members of the Prosecution team, but we very much oppose both applications. I believe it's in Rule 70 that the various work product of the OTP is not subject to disclosure. I think in this particular context fact that Mr. Tomljanovich is going to give evidence does not change that, and we again believe that all the matters that have been raised on application this afternoon, which could, of course, have been raised prior to today rather than at this late moment, should be denied and we should go forward in the usual manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond briefly. Firstly we could not have raised the privilege issue before because until Mr. Tomljanovich was worn as a witness it didn't arise. Your Honour, clearly once he becomes a witness, while there may have been work product and legal privilege before that point, the Prosecution has waived it by opening him up as they effectively concede by saying that we would be entitled to cross-examine. If I can cross-examine about his conversations with Mr. Scott, then clearly there is no privilege on that subject. And it's our submission, Your Honour, that we in the interests of both efficiency and legal entitlement we should be able to see any written work product that he may have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you have seen, we've very quickly reflected on this issue that we're very familiar with because we've discussed it for quite some day with regard to disclosure and the privilege issues. We believe after deliberation that there is no reason for the Defence to be given the internal memos that might have been exchanged between the members of the Office of the Prosecutor, since, and I'd like to read Rule 70(A): "Notwithstanding the provisions of Rule 66 and 67 reports, memoranda or other internal documents prepared by a party," in this case the Prosecutor, "it's assistance or representatives in connection with the investigation or preparation of the case are not subject to disclosure or notification under those Rules." That's the first part of my answer. The second part is something that the Judges have discussed as well. It's been asked for the witness to answer a number of questions that you've -- a list of which you've given us at the last minute. Let me count them. There are in total 60 questions. We take note of the fact that these questions deal with matters that can be raised during cross-examination, education, training, experience, employment at the Office of the Prosecutor, functions, works of the witness -- how the witness worked in this case, his knowledge as an expert, and his own assessment. These are all issues that the witness will be able to deal with during the cross-examination. However, and now I'm talking to the witness, I'd like to say the following: You've taken the solemn declaration, so you are now the witness of the Chamber. For the next five days you are no longer an employee of the OTP. You are a witness, a witness for justice. So for the next five days and even for more than five days because that will cover this week and the beginning of next week, during all this time you shall have no contact with Mr. Scott or Ms. Carla Del Ponte about this specific case, this present case in order to avoid any interference, any impressions. If we were to find out there had been contacts then it might be a case for contempt of court with a possible sentence of up to seven years. This being said, Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've already told us that you were born on the 17th of May, 1966. Can you tell us where you were born, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I was born in St. Paul Minnesota in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us about your undergraduate and graduate education.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: As an undergraduate I attended Columbia University and obtained a Bachelor of Arts degree in history and I obtained my Ph.D. then from Yale University in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In both under grad and in your graduate degree at Yale, did you have any particular of specialty or emphasis?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, both as an under graduate and as a graduate. As an under graduate I worked with my advisor Dr. Istvam Deak and concentrated on East Central European history in the modern period, which is also what my speciality was in graduate school, the Austrian Empire and its successor states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you proceeded on to Yale, did you do your -- a Ph.D. Or do a thesis on any particular topic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My topic was Bishop Josip Strossmayer, who was the bishop of Djakovo in Croatia from 1850 to 1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've already heard this afternoon, of course there's no dispute, that you are employed by the Office of the Prosecutor here at the ICTY. I will come back to that in a moment. When did you graduate from Yale with your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you do between receiving your degree -- let me put this this way. Can you tell us a bit about your employment and significant projects that you did before coming to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: From 1989 into 1996, I was teaching in different capacities at Yale University. As an assistant, teaching my own seminars, and also teaching my own courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On what topics or subjects?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: A number of different topics in history. Within my own narrow field of speciality I taught history of the Balkans in the modern period. I taught a seminar on nationalism in the Austrian Empire in its last century. I should also add that from 1998 to 1999, I also taught at Dickenson College in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, and both in Dickenson and at Yale I taught survey courses on modern European history.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your work or activities since studying at Yale, working at Yale, you've told us, as a teacher or assistant, have you also published a book?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. My dissertation or at least the dissertation was the basis for my book on Strossmayer, which was translated into Croatian and published in Croatia. I'm not sure if it was 2001 or 2002 that it actually came out, but somewhere around there that it was actually released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you came to the ICTY at what time, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: My first day in the office here was the 2nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly the nature of the kind of work that you do at the OTP, and how does it relate to your training, your education and training?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I'm a member of an office in the office -- investigations section called the Leadership Research Team. All members of the team have advanced degrees in something having to do with the former Yugoslavia, and all of us are capable of doing work in B/C/S as well. As a result, our work is very heavily focused on documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just mention a couple of things, sir. First of all, I know you're trying to assist the interpreters with going quite slow?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You might be able to go a bit more quickly perhaps. Secondly, you mentioned that you -- you and your colleagues are capable of doing work in B/C/S. Can you just confirm to the Judges, do you speak and write and read the -- what we call here at the Tribunal B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And have you been able, in fact, in the context of doing your work, a substantial amount of the documents that you've been able to review you've been able to review and work with them in the original language, that is B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. Generally speaking, we work with the original documents if they are in B/C/S. In B/C/S, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were in the courtroom a few minutes ago, sir, when it was mentioned that perhaps a training or background in political science might be more relevant to the work that you have done. Can you tell us how your training and work as an historian relates to the work that you do at the OTP and also the work that you've done before coming to the OTP, how that relates or is similar or not to the work you do at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It's extremely similar, because since the spring of 2000, I've been largely engaged in finding, acquiring, analysing, and organising archival materials, which is very similar to what I was doing as an historian. As a matter of fact, a great deal of the evidence that's in my report was found by myself and others in the same archive in which I was working as a historian in 1992, 1993. The process of selecting relevant documentation from a very large collection of archival materials is extremely similar whether or not the material is extremely recent or whether or not it's 150 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, what are some of the problems or challenges with working with such document collections, whether old or more recent?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, at different stages there's different problems. The first problem is knowing where to look in a large archival collection for the relevant materials. Once you've found them, a problem is, generally speaking and certainly with the collections we're going to talk about here, the greatest problem we've had is the enormous volume of materials we've had access to since the spring of 2000. Being able to find relevant materials within such large collections is very difficult. Once those materials are found, there's also a great deal of work cataloguing and classifying the documents so that they will be available to all persons who may need to make use of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've told us about -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Just very quickly. Once we have all these documents in house, the challenge is synthesising and analysing those documents which is already -- which is still a large amount of documentation and trying to present it in a coherent and concise fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are there any additional considers [sic] or methodology that you bring to your work as an historian in working with a document such as the ones that you have used here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, as I've already mentioned, I've had experience working with archives and archival materials, experience working with large amounts of materials and synthesising them, and probably more important than anything you learn in terms of methodology as a historian with this material, or in any material you find, what's very important is knowing the background and knowing the context of the documents you're looking at because the historical documents, whether it's from the 1990s or the 1860s, these -- this material wasn't written for the purpose of telling you what it is you want to find out, and that material has a great deal of assumed knowledge between the persons communicating. So a very good knowledge of the context in which these documents were put together and also a knowledge of how to synthesise all of these documents and present them coherently is something which once again it's very similar -- it's a very similar process in writing a book and also in writing this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, turning specifically to the nature of the report itself and the preparation of it, let me ask you this, and again you're in a courtroom this afternoon where certain questions have been raised, can you tell the Judges, sir, is there anything about your approach or the methodology or the work that you did in connection with your report or about observations that you have made in your report that in your view would be any different if you had performed this work while not employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: No, with one very clear exception. I can't imagine I'd be able to look at as much of this material and have as much time to get to know this much material this well if I hadn't been working here full time for seven and a half years. But other than that, I didn't reach -- I don't think -- if I'd been, say, an academic expert looking at these things from the outside, I can't imagine how it would have been any different or how my conclusions would have been any different, insofar as there are conclusions. I tried very hard not to put any of my own opinions into this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in that regard, then, again turning to your report, can you tell the Judges essentially what the -- what commission you received, if we can use that terminology, or what assignment were you given in terms of what report to prepare; that is, what to address and include in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. It was you yourself, Mr. Scott, who asked me, I think it was in November of last year, to present a report to the Judges explaining the political and governmental structures and processes of the HVO in its various incarnations, the -- or of Herceg-Bosna and its various incarnations, the HVO, the HZ HB, and the HR HB in the period from roughly middle 1991 to early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, briefly give us an overview of the scheme and structure of your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. The scheme and the structure is my own. What I decided to do is to begin the report starting off with the basic legislation that established governing organs and prescribed the function of governing organs in Herceg-Bosna in 1991, 1992, and for that first section I rely very heavily on documents from the Official Gazettes where this is laid out. In the next section, I look at how these organs actually functioned in practice from about August of 1992 until the fall of 1993 and beyond, looking very closely at main -- the main collection of documents that I'm looking at is not only the Official Gazettes again but also minutes of the meetings of the HVO HZ HB. Then in the third section, I go back to de jure mode and talk about the new organs or the changes in the existing organs of government as the HR HB was created in late 1993, early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the Official Gazette --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we've been told to do just the opposite of what I told you to do, Mr. Tomljanovich. If you could slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned already the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community or Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Is that something called the Narodni List?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Official Gazette -- Narodni List was the Official Gazette for both the HZ HB and the HR HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges and perhaps they know from some other training or experiences they've had, but when you describe this as an Official Gazette in this context, what is that or what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It's the public organ in which government organs, in this case the HVO HZ HB, the Presidency of the HZ HB, various departments make public various decrees and pronouncements and decisions so that other organs of government subordinate to them and so that other persons in the public are aware of the legislation that's been passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you explain the way that the Gazettes were used specifically in your experience and based on your study in Herceg-Bosna and the HVO and how they were organised and published?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Narodni List itself was a public company which was run by the HVO HZ HB. Periodically they would issue issues of this -- of their Gazette, numbered issues, periodically. There was no regular time frame in which it had to be done in which all of the official pronouncements -- all the official pronouncements designated for publication in the Narodni List were made. These tend to be in terms of volume -- most of this comes from the HVO HZ HB, although that is fair amount from the Presidency of the HZ HB, and then during the HR HB there's more legislation coming from organs outside of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was the -- is there a compilation of the Narodni List that is put together and published, if you will, on an annual basis in the sense of, can we go and say this is the Narodni List for 1992?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. I have bound copies of the Gazettes in my bookshelf, and when they're all put together, 1992 is about this thick. 1993 is a little thicker, and 1994 is two fairly thick volumes. Those are publicly available and were intended to be publicly available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might just mention to Your Honours at this time that what has been put together in one of the large bundles not for each Judge because some of this was -- because again of the volume of the material, but in the overall complete set of materials Exhibit P 00947 is the complete Narodni List for 1992, which I'll ask the witness to confirm. Exhibit P 05166 is the complete Narodni List for 1993, and Exhibits, two exhibits, P 07435 and P 07439, two volumes, comprise the complete Narodni List for 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tomljanovich, can you just confirm for purposes of the record that that is the case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in that respect, Your Honours, the Court has then for those three years the entire publications of the Official Gazettes of the HVO or the Community or Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Now, if we might take one example, exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you -- following the president's invitation, could you tell the Chamber you plan to put these into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We intend to put all these every -- document I specifically raise in my examination we intend put into evidence but yes, these particular documents we do so intend. I might further explain to Your Honours that the way the material has been organised is that, of the big bundles, the ones where there's only one set for everyone because of the volume, the 1992 for instance complete set is on top. In that -- then underneath that or in that schedule are selected translated individual items that are most relevant to the case. The Chamber hopefully will understand that there is a great volume -- a great amount of material that is completely irrelevant to this case, so this is -- what we consider the most relevant portions or passages have been translated and then given individual exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in order to gain time, when you're asking the witness a question on any particular paragraph, you will give us the number of the paragraph and the number of the page, please, because that will facilitate matters and it's that that is going to be tendered and then admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we could just starred as one example, if I could have displayed, please, Exhibit P 00305 in e-court. I suggest to Your Honours that for purposes of this particular explanation it might -- I thought it would be helpful to show one particular example of what the material looks like and then I'll explain the organisation of the remainder of the material as we turn to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can see what is displayed there sir, Mr. Tomljanovich, as P 00305, do you recognise this as an item in the format and style that you've seen published in the Narodni List that we've been talking about so far this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact can you tell the Judges what the particular topic or subject of this particular entry or item is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is the decision establishing and founding the Official Gazette, Narodni List, as reprinted in the Narodni List from -- I don't see the -- I think it's July 3rd, although I'm not sure. I can't see the date. If I could scroll down. Yes, it is. 3rd of July, 1992, signed by Mate Boban who was then the president of the HZ HB and the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, with that -- that covers for a moment, if you will, introduces the Narodni List material. Can I ask you then to describe, please -- you mention another set of materials that you used concerning the minutes or records of a particular body.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which body is that and which records are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the meetings of the HVO HZ HB and the cabinet of the HR HB, as well as the invitations to the meetings which contain the agendas to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On some of this material, sir, it's a bit like the chicken and an egg. It's where you start. You've several times used the abbreviations for example, the HVO HZ HB so far in your testimony. We're going to come to that in a few minutes in a rather substantial way but can you tell the Judges when you use that terminology the, HVO HZ HB, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, the HVO HZ HB was also colloquially known even during that period as the cabinet of the HVO HZ HB. It's the body of the president with his six department heads responsible for various fields of activity like defence and internal affairs and this is the body that then becomes the cabinet of the HR HB in late 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What kind of documents or records did this particular body then generate that you have described as using for purposes of your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, they generated minutes of their meetings. They generated agendas. They generated various decisions and decrees which are sometimes reprinted in the Official Gazettes but not always. In some instances we have them in original copies, not reprinted in the Gazettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, then there is a third bundle or stock of exhibits or material that has been provided to the Judges and then under a separate schedule, and is it correct, sir, that this -- these are all the documents referenced in your report other than Narodni List material or material related to the HVO cabinet?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe there was also a shorter list of those documents, simply the ones that had been highlighted that was put forward, which I received a copy of just a day or two ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point just so the Court is clear, for further reference what we will now be using for the remainder of Mr. Tomljanovich's examination-in-chief, and I suppose it's possible exception that something may have been left out and we will have to go to the very large collection, but will be the selected exhibits of that been put together in a separate set of materials for each of the Judges, each of the four Judges, and it is the set of materials starting -- the first exhibit is P 0069. And there is a schedule or should be of those documents, and the last document in that bundle or related that should be Exhibit P 09551.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, turning then to your report, can you tell us, please, at the time that the Bosnian Croat regional communities and Herceg-Bosna were being established, were there similar developments involving some of the other national or ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, there were. At the same time in late 1991, under the auspices of the Serbian nationalist political party SDA [sic], various municipalities formed what was known as Serbian autonomous regions using as their pretext for doing so the 1974 constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina which allowed for communities of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me correct you for a moment. I believe a moment ago in the transcript, or it came across as "SDA"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: SDS?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would carry on and tell us about these municipalities of communities.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This was being done in response to the prospect of Bosnia and Herzegovina leaving Yugoslavia. These communities reorganised themselves and eventually joined together into one political unit over the course of 1991 and 1992 with the intent of giving the SDS control of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And along this -- around this time, were some entities established, something that had been called the Serb autonomous areas?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the groupings of municipalities which I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately when, sir, were these bodies coming into existence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Without looking at my report, off the top of my head I'm just sure that this was done over the course of 1991, and in later 1991, these groups of municipalities were consolidating into a smaller number of larger groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could at this time provide in fact Mr. Tomljanovich with a copy of his report for his -- so that when we talk about the report he will have it to make reference to. With the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that is being done, he's being given his report, may I invite Mr. Scott to have the witness clarify one thing. The witness has already earlier stated that he's tried his best to keep his personal opinions out of his report, but he testified that the Serbian autonomous areas were created with a certain intent and I wonder if the witness could clarify what the basis of that opinion is about the intent of those who would create those organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, you've heard the question of counsel?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'd like to make any further comment on that, please do so.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, in discussing the Serb autonomous regions which was only intended to be background information to put the other material in context, I looked at a number of documents which are cited here in my report. The footnotes 3 to 14. And what -- all of what I relied on is there, although I should add that as far as the background material is concerned, I was trying to speed up the background, and I'm not focusing as narrowly on each document with the background as I do with the body of the paper once we get to the HZ HB and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us approximately when the entity that's known as the Republika Srpska, when that entity was formed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, that's a good question. You see, I have it in my report, although off the top of my head I do not remember. Well, the Bosnian Serb Assembly was formed on 24th of October, 1991. The plebiscite of Serb municipalities on remaining in Yugoslavia then followed from the 9th and 10th of November, 1991, and Republika Srpska, I don't believe -- I don't think that's in my paper, the declaration of Republika Srpska, although I could be wrong. I believe that was not until 1992, but I'm not sure off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we're not going to talk about the next set of exhibits in any great detail because I think the Chamber may have -- they've been covered with other witnesses the Chamber has already heard. Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 00069. And for reference -- for the courtroom's reference and your -- if you will assist you, Mr. Tomljanovich, I think some of this material is covered at pages 10 to 13 of your report. Can you just tell us briefly what this document is, sir, and whether you considered it in fact as included in the body of your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. I cited this document in my report. This is a meeting of the 12th of November, 1991, held in Grude with the members of the Crisis Staffs of two different regional communities, of the HDZ BiH, one from Travnik, which represented Central Bosnia, and the Crisis Staff from Herzegovina. The two meet on this day. The Presiding Officers were their respective presidents, Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Dario Kordic, and at this meeting they voiced their intention to form a union of the two regional communities into one regional community, and they describe some of their reasons for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we next show the witness, please, Exhibit P 00079. MR. SCOTT: And I will confirm, Mr. President, which of these documents were already admitted. If they have not -- if any of them -- the ones of -- that have not been admitted, they will be tendered at the conclusion of Mr. Tomljanovich's evidence. And can you -- if you have that -- it's not up yet. Can you please tell us briefly what that document is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is one of the many copies we have of the decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or HZ HB which was done on 18th of November, 1991. If we scroll down to Article 2, it sets the territory of Herceg-Bosna as including those municipalities. If we can scroll down to Article 5. Yes. The HZ HB recognises the democratic -- will recognise that they respect the democratically elected government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as it is independent to any future or former Yugoslavia. In Article 7, finally, it states that the leadership of the community will be the Presidency which will consist of representatives of the Croatian people in the municipal government and the senior members or presidents of the municipal boards of the HDZ or Croatian Democratic Union and that that body will have itself a president, vice-president, and a secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, with reference -- as referenced on page 14 of your report, can I ask you -- ask that you please be shown Exhibit P 00152. And can you tell the Judges, please, what was the effect or -- what was the effect of this document and when was this? Maybe with the assistance of the usher we can scroll down further and indicate the date of this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, the date of this decision is the 8th of April, 1992. It's signed by Mate Boban on behalf of the Presidency of the HZ HB, which enacted this, it says in the preamble, enacted this decision at an emergency session on 8th of April, 1992. And this decision creates the HVO HZ HB as the supreme defence body of the Croatian people in the HZ HB. One other thing I should probably add, under Article 2 it lists that its objectives shall be to take care of the sovereign space of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and to protect the Croatian people as well as other peoples in the community attacked by an aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened as a result based on your study and the documents you've looked at, what entity or what operation was put into existence as a result of this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: The HVO HZ HB, as well as the affiliate organs were put into existence on the basis of this document but not immediately, and specific -- the specific parameters of what was going to be established were set in later decisions which followed upon this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. As covered on pages 14 to 16 of your report, could I also ask you please be shown Exhibit P 09526?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if may interject here while this is happening. I'm unable to follow exactly what is the purpose of this kind of direct examination. You have a report that was generated by the gentleman. The report is footnoted citing the authorities that he's relying on. We're not getting a narration from the gentleman. Now, I assume Mr. Scott is going to be tendering the entire report. So perhaps we could get a narration from the gentleman and then he could maybe then look at particular documents for context, but he indicated that when he drafted the report that he took into consideration background and context. I neither hear background nor do I see anything that he's saying being put into context. By that what I mean is, the background of the events, the context in which these documents were -- were drafted at the time what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, perhaps Mr. Scott will be getting to that, but I would think that it might be very helpful to the Trial Chamber in understanding what exactly this testimony is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I have to disagree with Mr. Karnavas. A few minutes ago, for example, the witness explained the context in which the founding documents of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna came about, that at the same time as that was happening various Serb autonomous areas and units and government entities were being put into place. That was putting this material in context. He also added just a moment ago information to the Chamber that although the exhibit P 00152 was adopted on the 8th of April, 1992, it was not in fact put into effect some time later. So I do not intend to cover the entire report which everyone has nor every document in the report, but we are trying to take the Chamber through significant parts of the report and Mr. Tomljanovich can add additional details and information as we go. The Chamber has indicated previously that in order for the exhibits to be admitted, the witness will have to address those exhibits. I would be happy to admit -- to tender all exhibits referenced in his report in their totality. But if that is not the Court's procedure then the way I propose to do and the way that I have prepared the examination based on the Court's prior rulings in this case is that I would take him through the most -- what I would consider the most important documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand correctly, you are submitting a number of documents quickly to the witness, and later on you'll move on to the substance of the report, to the context and to the pivotal issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you have now Exhibit P 09526 in front of you, can you tell us what that is? And again, I'm asking you to do in each instance, Mr. Tomljanovich, is then, when the document is shown, connect it to your report and explain to the Judges the value or the role, if you will that that particular document played in the analysis that you've given to the Judges by way of your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. This document here, in the original it's handwritten notes from a meeting of the Presidency of the HVO HZ HB from the 15th of May, 1992. This is also the meeting at which they passed the first version of the statutory decision on executive government, and this document is minutes of that meeting which reveals their thinking behind doing that and their political motivations for creating an executive organ, which is what they're doing, creating an executive organ to govern the territory of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any sort of founding documentation, if you will, besides these -- besides the one document we looked at, the decision, and these notes as to the structure and authorities of this body that became known as the HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, yes. The first document, which is a sort of constitutional -- or sort of constitutional document, is the statutory decision which is passed at this meeting on the 15th of May, 1992, which is significantly revised on the 3rd of July, 1992, at the next meeting of the Presidency of the HVO HZ HB. In the intervening period there was also a law governing the function of municipal governments within the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could I ask that the witness be shown, please, Exhibit P 00303.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, is this a copy of the document that you referred to a moment ago when you said in your testimony -- you said the statutory decision on executive authority?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, this is. This is the revised version of the 3rd of July, 1992, as it appears in Narodni List.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The earlier document that we looked at from April, on the 8th of April, 1992, described the HVO as the supreme defence body. How does this statutory decision describe the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, in Article 1 here it describes the HVO as the supreme executive and administrative body in the HZ HB. If you look down further, it's described as a temporary body. Its members are made accountable to the Presidency much in a fashion that any ordinary cabinet would be in other systems would be accountable to the parliament. It -- under -- let me see here. Sorry. Under Article 7, it lists the members of the HVO. Moving further down to the next page, article 9 defines the powers of the president of the HVO, stating that he shall be in charge of the work of the HVO and held accountable for it and ensuring the unity of the mythical administrative of the HVO and coordinating with other bodies and organisations of the HVO HZ HB, and also stating that he'll sign the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, can you confirm to the Judges during the time of its creation, from the time of this statute and its creation are put into place until August of 1993 when at least formally the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was changed to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, who was the president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: From its beginning until August of 1992, that was Mate Boban, who was simultaneously the president of the HZ HB and the president of the Presidency. From August of 1992 onwards, that was Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention for a moment back to Article 6. It says "the HVO shall regulate the activities, structure, operational framework and powers of its departments in accordance with the regulations passed by the Presidency."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What are the departments being discussed there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: The HVO in legislation which followed right after this had six departments. Department of Defence, Department of Internal Affairs, Department of Social Welfare and the Family, Department of Justice and General Administration, Department of Finance, and the Department of Economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In Article 3, which I believe you mentioned a moment ago, you said "The HVO" -- it says, excuse me, "The HVO and the HZ HB and every HVO member are accountable to the Presidency of the HZ HB." Now, I'm going to ask you to assist the Judges now, sir, because the term "Presidency" will appear in different usages and contexts, and can you tell the Judges now, describe for them the different way in which the term "Presidency" is used and which bodies it refers to.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. It's only -- seems confusing because it is. The Presidency of the HZ HB is this legislative body which is set up in November of 1991 containing representatives of all of the different municipalities, and that's more or less an Assembly and functions as a parliament until its last meeting in October of 1992. There's the president of the Presidency. It has a presiding officer. So there's the president of the Presidency, then there's also the president of the HZ HB, which is Mate Boban. At the same time, the HVO HZ HB also has its own president whose office is sometimes referred to in translations as the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. The statutory decision refers to this body as of 1992 as being in Article 2 a temporary body. Can you tell the Judges, please, on the basis of your work whether this was a temporary body and in fact how long Herceg-Bosna and the HVO continued to exist, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: The HZ HB ceases to exist in August of 1993 when it's supplanted by the HR HB although there is continuity between the HZ HB and the HR HB, a great deal of continuity, and the HVO HZ HB becomes the cabinet of the HR HB. In one form or another, these organisations exist well past the Dayton agreement. As far as the question of temporary is concerned, it's temporary until August of 1993 -- or, actually, 20th November, 1993, when HVO offices are done away with in favour of the succession -- and are succeeded by HR HB offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that does not actually happen, if I heard you correctly, until November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned in my report. There is a transitional period from the declaration of the HR HB in late August, 1993, to 20th of November, 1993, when all of the old offices and job descriptions are done away with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next to look at Exhibit P 00440, with the usher's assistance on e-court. Mr. Tomljanovich, could you give the Judges an overview of this document, please, and point out the particular aspects of it that most directly relate to your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is the decree on the organisation and responsibilities of the departments and commissions of the HVO of the HZ HB. I'm not sure of the exact date since I can't see the bottom of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a multi-page document.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Although I think I remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I hope it wouldn't be in dispute that on the last page of the document it says the 14th of August --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: 14th of August. Yes it was passed on the 14th of August, 1992, and signed by Mate Boban as the president of the HVO and HZ HB. And what this does is it gives the description of the duties and spheres of spot for the six departments we just mentioned, with different departments in many instances subdepartments under them are created, and the responsibilities and duties of those subdepartments are also listed here. There's three commissions of the HVO HZ HB which are also created in this document, commission on regulations, the commission on transformation of property, and also for rebuilding and reconstruction. It also defines the duties of each of the department heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can just go a bit more specifically to, for example, Article 8 on the second page. You, a moment ago, listed the departments as they existed at that time. Is this an accurate list, then, of the departments of the HVO as of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There's different ways that the names can be translated into English, but these are the six departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for example, if the Judges care to, if they look at Article 9, that will set out essentially the mandate or functions of the Department of Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. And each of the other departments follows in succession in the next few articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to be shown Article 31. And for -- it has the ERN page. If it assists for e-court being 00840728. Yes, there is it is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges how does this particular Article 31 enter into your report, and how did you find this to be carried out according to the documentary accounts, the documentary history of these organisations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this structure, in fact, followed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, it was, in fact. What they're talking about here is that the department heads will have deputies and that they'll be appointed by the Presidency of the HZ HB at the proposal of the HVO HZ HB. Now, this follows a general principle you see here in Herceg-Bosna that appointments were made by the second-instance supervisor at the recommendation of the first-instance supervisor. So for example an assistant minister of defence would be appointed by the HVO HZ HB at the recommendation of the head of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in addition to -- because we will see was we continue into your report and your testimony, in addition to departments were there other administrative bodies or organisations that were used by the HVO or the Herceg-Bosna structures to carry out various parts of its work -- their work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few. And the founding legislation allows the HVO HZ HB to create extra commissions and other extra bodies to deal with things they need done as they see fit, and certainly this was done over the course of the HVO HZ HB. A number of other bodies were created in order to serve specific functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could quickly go on to the next document, then, Exhibit 684 -- or P 00684. Can you tell us about this -- first of all, tell us what it is and then tell us how this affected the -- the way that the HVO did business during this time.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. This is an extremely important piece of legislation. It's the amendment, and if I could just scroll down to get the exact wording. This is the decision amending the statutory decision on the provisional organisation of executive power, which, as I mentioned, established the rules for the operation of the HVO HZ HB and its duties and sphere of activity. Now, what this decision does, and it's signed by Mate Boban after the last meeting of the Presidency of the HZ HB, and this allows, if we could scroll down a little bit further into Article 1, this changes Article 18 of the statutory decision and it allows the HVO HZ HB to pass legislation in the sphere of responsibility of the Presidency of the HZ HB. And what this essentially does it takes over the powers of legislature and provisionally gives them to the HVO HZ HB and allows them to enact legislation in that field of responsibility. And this is invoked fairly frequently thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to read or take anyone's time to read each one but in the second clause or paragraph, if you will, Article 1 it says "In the exercise of its powers the HVO shall adopt decrees, decisions, dispositions and conclusions." And my question, sir, is that, are each of those then further defined in the remaining part of the decision?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just by way of a quick overview, is essentially -- a decree is something that has a general application, something that we might generally call -- some of us might call a statute or a law?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It was binding, yes. The distinctions between those four sorts of enactments not being a lawyer I'm not completely clear what the distinctions are. It's stated there for anyone to read, though, exactly what the distinctions are, but all of those are binding, and they have the power to enforce all of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time. If the Court would like to take a break at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a break, 20-minute break. We'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges based on your work and then we'll look at some -- continuing with particular documents, did you find that the authorities and functions -- that the authorities and functions that were carried out by the HVO HZ HB increased and centralised more and more HVO authority in that body over time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. In their own semi-annual report the HVO HZ HB makes reference to the fact that their sphere of authority in late 1992 was constantly expanding. And there is a number of references in the minutes of the meetings of the HVO HZ HB where individual members complain that the Presidency of the HZ HB isn't taking -- filling its functions as a policy-making body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard can I ask you to look at -- or to be shown Exhibit P 00128. And if I can -- if we can scroll down the page, please. If we can go back to the English version, please, and scroll down. Mr. Tomljanovich, can you please indicate to the Judges language that you see in this document you may need to refer to, continue on to other pages, that is consistent with or supports what you stated just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, but scroll down a little bit so I can see all of the last paragraph in English. This is what I was talking an about earlier, it says that, "The HVO HZ HB was founded in May 1992 as the highest body of executive authority and administration ..." And then as it goes further yes, at the bottom it begins, "However, in time, the obligations were expanded --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hold on one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. I should explain first of all, too, before we get into that, this is a semi-annual report of the HVO HZ HB. It's a compilation the cover was done by the HVO HZ HB itself and it's compilation of the various reports of the various departments of the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and you're absolutely right to point that out. Did the HVO establish a practice or adopt a practice of issuing a report summarising its activities in six-month increments?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely and we've entered -- I've used in my report the semi-annual report for 1992 and the two semi-annual reports for 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the report that we're looking at now, which is Exhibit P 00128, this is the report that covers the period from the foundation of the HVO HZ HB up until the end of calendar year 1992, that is the 31st of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking, individual departments and offices may for whatever internal reasons they have periodise things a little bit differently but it's supposed to be for the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, with that additional background in mind could you please go to the bottom of page 1 where you began to read a moment ago, starting with the word "however," and continue on, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: "However, in time the above rights and obligations were expanded to a full legislative function, because by a change of the statutory decision the earlier right to pass regulations within its own sphere was --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. " ... was expanded to include the passing of regulations within the mandate of the Presidency of the HZ HB. Since for the passing of regulations it is necessary to define one's own political orientation and views, responsibility for determining policies in all spheres was, in effect, transferred to a certain extent to the HVO HZ HB."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, turning for a moment to some of the early appointments in this -- the structures that we've been looking at so far this afternoon -- and I've been reminded to offer these exhibits, tender these exhibits as we go, so I'll try to begin doing that. We tender Exhibit P 00128. And if I could next ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P 00208. Can you tell us what that document is, sir, and what it does?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is a translation of a decision which was printed and reprinted in Narodni List appointing Jadranko Prlic head of the finance department of the HVO HZ HB on the 15th of May, 1992, and signed by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could we go then next to Exhibit P 00308. And can you tell us what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is the 3rd July, 1992, appointment of Bruno Stojic as the head of the defence department. I believe this is also signed by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And based on your report and research, sir, is it correct that Mr. Stojic remained in this position as the chief of the defence department, albeit at some point the terminology changed to the Ministry of Defence, until approximately November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It's my understanding that he stayed at this position until the position itself ceased to exist on the 20th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We tender, Your Honours, Exhibit P 00208 and P 00308.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just have a point of clarification here. I assume, maybe I'm assuming incorrectly, but I assume that the gentleman's report will be introduced in total, because he's an expert. And it would seem to me, I don't know how my colleagues feel, but at least my experience is, because everything in the report is referenced and is cited to some sort of documents, normally all of the documents would necessarily come in with the report. I'm just stating that as -- that has been the practice, as I understand it, you know, as opposed to going, you know -- as the Prosecutor is doing right now. And if indeed the report is accepted for -- such as it is, at least from my point of view I would not be objecting to anything that's cited to also come in as part of the report, because I don't think that you can just look at the report and then some of the documents, all of the citations, would necessarily be part of the report. That lays a foundation. I don't know if I'm complicating matters, but just that I thought I would mention that. That has been the practice in other -- in other cases. I don't know how my colleagues feel. I assume Mr. Scott will tell us whether he intends to introduce the report. If so, I personally have no objections on everything that's cited as a basis for an opinion to also being introduced, you know. Keeping in mind that we can also always challenge the authenticity or the reliability of the document later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We take note of what you've said, and it's along the lines of what we were saying. It will enable us to save time. But the procedure that Mr. Scott is applying emanates from our decision of the 28th of April, 2006, where we said in paragraph (k) that if an expert witness produces a report it can be tendered with respect to pertinence and probative value. The Chamber will only admit the reports and exhibits when the witness is present and testifies. So, for example, if the report is not tendered and you challenge it, then this entails the other documents as well. If the document is not admitted into evidence, then some of the documents will be. So if you're not challenging the report, then everything is fine. We can save time in that way and proceed in that way, because there are quite a lot of documents that you're not going to challenge at all. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... clear. First of all, we're challenging the gentleman as being capable of actually generating a report that would be considered as an expert report. We feel that he's not an expert. He's testified previously as an analyst. He can testify as an analyst and as a fact witness. So we don't see that, his report, as having any value. Keeping -- that being said, we understand also that -- that the Court has already deemed him to be an expert and will give whatever weight it deems necessary to his testimony subsequent to hearing the evidence, you know, of this entire case. That being said, I certainly am not -- I certainly object to the report coming in, and I object to the gentleman testifying in this capacity, but it seems that the Court has already made a decision, that he is an expert, and I assume his report is coming in. The manner in which the direct examination is being done now, I see very little value of how the Trial Chamber can understand the gentleman's testimony without referencing or at least reading the report. I just -- I don't see the purpose of it. So I don't think -- and I don't want to be flip about this, but there's no sense in doing this kabuki dance that is being done. The Prosecutor can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rest assured, Mr. Karnavas, we've already read the report and in fact we've read it several times. So we know the report. You don't need to worry about that. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, continue, but always quote the exhibit that you're asking your questions on so we can take note of that. There are exhibits that are not subject to any discussion, such as the appointment of Mr. Stojic, unless that is wrong, and I'd be surprised, but if that is challenged, then it's up to the cross-examination. So that's why we need you to tell us the exhibits with the numbers and then the cross-examination can -- during the cross-examination the Defence can say they don't agree and then we'll be able -- they'll be able to ask their own questions. But at this stage we can't make any ruling or decision about anything. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think Your Honour has just cleared it up. I may have misunderstand Mr. Karnavas's point, but I do want to make it clear that as far as the Stojic Defence is concerned, at least, we don't accept that a document is necessarily authenticated and becomes admissible simply because it's mentioned in the expert report, and we would submit that the proper practice still remains that which has been laid down in the evidence decision rendered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Quite. Yes, you're quite right to raise that point. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward, sir, you told us some minutes ago that although the decision adopting or creating the HVO HZ HB was adopted in, I think it was initially April of 1992, there -- did not begin fully operating until sometime later. Can you tell us when and under what circumstances according to your research this body began to operate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, again, this is something referred to in that same semi-annual report, but until Mr. Prlic was appointed as the president of the HVO HZ HB, the HVO HZ HB did not begin having regular meetings and regular numbered meetings. And this is also borne out by the meetings and their numbering, that the regular meetings of the HVO HZ HB and its function really began in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P 00429. I must tell the Judges for whatever reason this one was not included in the smaller bundle, but it's a very short document and you'll see it momentarily, Exhibit P 00429. And if we could scroll down just a bit, please. Sir, according to your research, as published in the Narodni List is this a copy or the record of decision appointing Mr. Prlic as president of the HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 14th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, and signed by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that it was around this time when this body began functioning on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. The first numbered meeting of the HVO HZ HB takes place within days of this. I forget the exact date, but it's only days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you give the Judges some idea of how things changed in the way that this body actually operated on the appointment of Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: From that day forward, from middle of August onwards, the HVO HZ HB met on at least a weekly basis. They had numbered meetings about once a week at which they dealt with proposed legislation and proposals to discuss matters from the different members of the HVO HZ HB.
